text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, how the quality of your diet is probably more important
than obsessing on the individual parts of it. Drugs in palliative care which make
distress worse and can even kill you. An investment strategy for the government
which could tap into potential earnings of around $60 billion. Not bad money
when the bean counters are looking for every cent. And how optimism can save
your life. A 70,000-person study has linked optimism to around a 30% reduction
in the risk of premature death from any cause. The lead author is Eric Kim of the
Harvard School of Public Health in Boston. Welcome to the Health Report.

Eric Kim: Thank you.

Norman Swan: What did we know about optimism and its relation to life
expectancy, dying prematurely, before you did your study?

Eric Kim: There have been studies linking optimism with reduced risk of death
from coronary heart disease, cardiovascular outcomes. However there has never
been a study looking at different causative outcomes as well.

Norman Swan: We should have explained this at the beginning, but we think we
know what optimism is but maybe you should just explain it.

Eric Kim: In a nutshell it's the expectation that things will be better than worse,
and what's really interesting is that people think that optimistic people are just
always chipper and sunny people. However, what's also interesting is that people
might not necessarily present that way but have just the internal belief that things
will get better.

Norman Swan: So they're not necessarily happy chappies?

Eric Kim: Yes, but do believe things will get better.

Norman Swan: This is the Nurses' Study, which we've had on the Health
Report many times over the years. It's an extraordinary large study, tens of
thousands of women followed over decades, and you've obviously done a
psychological profile on these women and seen what happens to them.

Eric Kim: There's a well validated optimism measure, and it asks questions like
'in uncertain times I usually expect the best', or 'I hardly ever expect things to go
 
my way', and there are a series of questions like this and you can assess
someone's level of optimism. And then we have looked and tracked people's
survival over time as well as lots of other factors.

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Eric Kim: We found that when we looked at people with the highest optimism
versus the lowest lowest optimism, so the top 25 versus the bottom 25, the most
optimistic had about a 29% reduced risk of mortality, and we also controlled for
all kinds of different confounders and saw that the association kept persisting.

Norman Swan: When you say reduced risk of mortality, mortality is 100%, so
you're talking about reduced mortality at your particular age?

Eric Kim: Yes.

Norman Swan: Now we've got to dissect optimism, because some people who
are pessimistic are depressed.

Eric Kim: Yes. I also want to say something that I'm very passionate about and
have seen a little bit of, this idea of potential victim blaming. People can have low
optimism for all variety of reasons, some that are within our control, but also a lot
of factors that are not within our control such as parental warmth when someone
is younger actually predicts someone's optimism. Levels of education and wealth
is weak but it is a predictor of optimism as well.

Norman Swan: So I'm assuming with parental warmth you're talking about the
emotionally in-tune parent who sets limits but within a loving environment.

Eric Kim: Yes, something like that.

Norman Swan: And how much of it is genetic or really pre-programmed into your
personality?

Eric Kim: There has been some twin studies and it shows that about 25% of it is
heritable, which suggests that there are things that we can do to influence our
levels of optimism.
 
Norman Swan: So you've adjusted for all these things, your diet, whether you
are depressed, and you still find that optimism by itself seems to reduce your risk
particularly of heart disease and cancer and other causes of premature death.

Eric Kim: Yes.

Norman Swan: So what is it about optimism that does it?

Eric Kim: There are three potential pathways, and one is that optimism may
influence better health, for example. Past studies have shown that optimistic
people actually eat healthier, exercise more and acquire better sleep. And a
second pathway might be that optimists have better coping skills, and there is a
recent review of over 50 studies and they showed that optimists in general use
better coping methods, like they seek support more in stressful times, they plan
for challenges and they have more contingency plans, like if plan A doesn't go
well, then they plan for B and C. And the third potential pathway is that optimism
may actually directly influence our biology.

Norman Swan: It's that last one we've looked at a couple of times on the Health
Report, particularly looking at people who have already got cancer, and this
comes to your caveat a few moments ago which is that you can blame the
person for not being optimistic. So they looked at people with cancer in Australia
and then tracked them through according to their attitude, their mental attitude,
are they optimistic or pessimistic, and it made absolutely no difference to the
outcome once you had cancer because one of the problems is that if your cancer
comes back people say, oh well, you didn't have a positive enough attitude.

Eric Kim: I'm not aware of that particular study but these were healthier people
at baseline, and we weren't looking at people who had serious illnesses, so that
might be a different subset.

Norman Swan: So when you find this sort of association in a study like this, it's
not necessarily cause and effect. You try and find out whether it is but really all
you can say is the link is strong between optimism and a 30% reduced risk of
dying prematurely from all-cause mortality. So that's fine. But it's not cause and
effect yet. To prove it's cause and effect you change somebody from a
pessimistic attitude towards life to an optimistic view. Is there any evidence at all
that changing one's view of the world and life changes your mortality rate?
 
Eric Kim: I think there were three studies published in JAMA Internal Medicine,
and I'll tell you an example of one of them. There were people who had a heart
condition, they had a heart procedure, and over the period of a year they induced
positive emotions in one group, and the other half had standard of care. And in
the group were they induced positive emotions they were actually 1.7 times more
likely to achieve their physician recommended levels of physical activity. And the
other studies actually showed higher medication adherence and things like that.
So there are some really promising and interesting randomised control studies
where we can pinpoint causality, showing that when we induce these positive
mental states, that it could change our health behaviours.

Norman Swan: And are there reliable techniques for switching you to the
optimism mode?

Eric Kim: There are some easier ones that have smaller effect sizes and then
more time and resource intensive ones that have larger effect sizes and are more
reliable. I'll start with the easier ones first. One is just listing things that you are
grateful for every day, and randomised studies show that if you do it for seven
days then your optimism will increase a little bit. Another showed that if you list
things that you do that are kind over a period of 14 days, that could also increase
your optimism a bit.

Norman Swan: Where you have been kind to somebody else?

Eric Kim: Yes, listing your instances of kindness throughout the day. And then a
third one is called the best possible self, and you think about your different
domains of life, whether it be…maybe one domain is your relationship with your
partner or spouse, another one is your career and another one is your
friendships, and you think about the best possible outcome. Then the next six
days you vividly try to imagine that, that has also been shown to increase
optimism a bit. Some of the more resource and time intensive ones include
mindfulness meditation, different forms of cognitive behavioural therapy, and
something called hope therapy.

Norman Swan: So those require a bit more work but they do have a larger
effect.

Eric Kim: Yes.
 
Norman Swan: Eric Kim, thank you very much for joining us on the Health
Report.

Eric Kim: Thank you so much.

Norman Swan: Eric Kim is at the Harvard School of Public Health in Boston.

And in a related story be sure to listen to the next episode of All in the Mind when
Lynne Malcolm explores the field of social genomics, how adverse life
circumstances such as deep loneliness could increase the gene activity that
leads to chronic disease, and how having a sense of meaning in life can be
protective against disease. That's on Sunday afternoon at 5 o'clock and online on
Radio National.

Meantime you're with the Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio, and CBC
Radio across Canada.

Let's stay with keeping your mortal coil as healthy as possible for as long as
possible and move from your mind to your diet. Australian research has found
that focusing on your whole diet rather than obsessing on individual nutrients
pays off in terms of obesity and blood pressure, and that our official dietary
guidelines do seem to work, which no doubt has a lot of experts breathing a sigh
of relief. The bad news is that you still have to stay off junk food. Katherine
Livingstone of Deakin University did a lot of the work on this study and she is in
our Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Katherine Livingstone: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Why choose obesity and blood pressure?

Katherine Livingstone: So obesity and hypertension are really major health
problems facing the average Australia population. We know, for example, two in
every three adults are overweight or obese, and one in every three adults have
hypertension, and it is really potentially quite interesting, the relationship between
risk of obesity and hypertension and the combined effect, so up to 75% of
hypertension is thought to be caused by being overweight or obese. So if we are
able to understand how we can tackle these major health issues we can really
 
make a meaningful impact on the overall health of the population. Of course one
of the ways we can do this, as you said, is through diet.

Norman Swan: So you looked at the extent to which people…just tell us about
this study that you did.

Katherine Livingstone: So in this study we were looking at individuals following
the Australian dietary guidelines. As many of your listeners will know, the
Australian dietary guidelines provide really useful key information on the types
and the amounts of the foods that we should eat to promote health and well-
being. And I think what's really important to distinguish in these
recommendations is that we have things that we should eat more of in our diet,
so these are the beautiful fruits and the vegetables and the whole grains, and
things that we should limit, so things high in saturated fat and salt, so these
would be our crisps and our biscuits. And so these are fantastic clear messages
to the public. But what's really missing is evaluating how are these updated
recommendations that were issued in 2013 actually relate to these major health
problems of obesity and high blood pressure.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Katherine Livingstone: So in our study we included just under 5,000 men and
women, and it's important to know that these were individuals from all across
Australia, so all states and territories, really great, fantastic nationally
representative data, and we derived two overall dietary scores, and these were
both based on the Australian dietary guidelines but there's quite an important
difference in these two scores. So the first one is based on whether individuals
meet the recommendations for what they should eat more of, so these are the
fruits and the vegetables, but also what they should eat less of, so these are high
fat cakes and crisps for example. Whereas the second score we actually looked
at what would happen if individuals just met the recommended foods, so if they
just ate two portions of fruit, five of the vegetables, they matched their intakes of
wholegrain, of lean meats and low fat dairy. And actually what we saw was a
really important differentiation between these two scores, in that individuals were
only associated with lower risk of obesity if they had both recommended intakes
of the things that they should eat more off and the things that they should eat
less of. So this is an important message to the public.
 
Norman Swan: So it wasn't just that you could feel honourable by having your
two fruits and five veg or…I can't remember which way around it is, but that sort
of thing, and not much red meat and low saturated fat, you had to stay off the
rubbish.

Katherine Livingstone: That's right. So people really have to consider, yes,
we've had great amounts of fruit and vegetables but that doesn't mean that there
is an excuse then to go out and eat a whole block of chocolate. We've got to
keep that message of moderation in mind.

Norman Swan: So where does the dietary pattern fit into this? Because people
obsess, you know, something which we recorded for the Health Report at the
Sydney Writers Festival recently, we got 700 people or something in the
audience, we got them to put up their hands, how many are on a gluten-free diet,
and 80% put up their hands. How many are on low carbs, and 50% put up their
hands. People are obsessing on individual nutrients rather than the whole diet.
Presumably they are running the risk of not being on the right diet.

Katherine Livingstone: That's right, and there are a lot of what we call fad diets
or celebrity endorsed diets out there, and I think the key message coming from
this study is that simply by following these tried and tested scientifically robust
recommendations, that we are going to achieve a really great impact on
maintaining our weight and maintaining healthy blood pressure. So we shouldn't
be fixated, as you said, on these single foods and these single nutrients, and
that's what the focus of the revised 2013 Australian dietary guidelines was, much
more food based, overall diet based because, as you said, we don't just eat a
potato, we are going to eat that as part of a whole meal. We're going to have
maybe our vegetables and maybe our meat, and it's the impact of all of that
together that's important.

Norman Swan: And is there a translation to life expectancy here?

Katherine Livingstone: We didn't look at life expectancy particularly in this
study, but you would hope that with a lower risk of obesity and hypertension, that
that's going to have knock-on effects on life expectancy but we didn't look at that
specifically.
 
Norman Swan: And do we all have to then go to the National Health and Medical
Research Council's website to find out the dietary guidelines and go cross eyed,
or is there a simple way of doing this? People say it's the Mediterranean diet, not
a lot of red meat, white meat, monounsaturated fats et cetera, that sort of dietary
pattern. Is that what it all boils down to?

Katherine Livingstone: Yes, so the recommendations are up on the website, as
you said, but the key messages to the public is you really do want to have a wide
variety of foods, so great colours and different components in there. You want to
have plenty of vegetables, plenty of fruits, plenty of wholegrain foods, so for
example maybe once a week instead of having the white rice you'll have the
wholegrain rice, plenty of lean meat and eggs and legumes, low fat dairy
products and plenty of water. We are all tempted to maybe have the fizzy drink
now and then, maybe just swap that for water more often.

Norman Swan: And don't feel honourable and have a blowout.

Katherine Livingstone: Exactly, everything in moderation and balance.

Norman Swan: Katherine, thanks very much for joining us on the Health Report.

Katherine Livingstone: Thank you, it's a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Katherine Livingstone is in the Institute for Physical Activity and
Nutrition at Deakin University.

People who are receiving palliative care are understandably often really
distressed and that can manifest as confusion, disturbed communication and
even the feeling that you are hallucinating. That often gets doctors reaching for
drugs called antipsychotics, normally reserved for people with schizophrenia. But
these have been poorly researched in palliative care. A recent Australian study
though suggests that these medications may make distress worse and even
reduce survival. Meera Agar was the lead author. Meera is a palliative medicine
physician at the Centre for Cardiovascular and Chronic Care at the University of
Technology, Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report.

Meera Agar: Thank you.
 
Norman Swan: So just tell me the typical story here, the typical patient that
you're talking about.

Meera Agar: So we're talking about people with advanced illness where we know
there is no longer a cure for their underlying illness and that their life expectancy
is shortened. And we know that at least one in three of those people will have a
delirium episode at some point in their final months of life.

Norman Swan: So delirium being what I just described…maybe you should just
describe it in a bit more detail, because it is often missed by nursing and medical
staff.

Meera Agar: So delirium is a condition of the brain which is actually a medical
emergency. There are many medical issues that cause delirium, including
infection, changes in medication, changes in your body, metabolic states such as
liver or kidney failure. And what happens is a whole raft of symptoms, confusion,
agitation, hallucinations are often the most noticeable ones, but people's inability
to focus attention, inability to communicate, drowsiness are also a part of the
spectrum of delirium, and often those are the ones that get missed.

Norman Swan: So what you're saying is there are some symptoms…some
people can be acting out and seeing things and really being very distressed and
outward and hard to control in some ways, and other people can go very quiet.

Meera Agar: And sometimes it's just assumed that because these people have
an advanced illness, that it's okay to have a day where you are a bit quiet and a
bit down, and people often don't think that it might be delirium that's causing
those sudden changes.

Norman Swan: And when you say it's a medical emergency, why is it a medical
emergency?

Meera Agar: Because we need to actually try and assess what the underlying
medical condition is very quickly and get on top of those issues. So if someone
has an infection causing their delirium, we need to be trying to treat that quickly
and expediently because the longer it has effects on the brain, the poorer the
outcomes for the delirium will be.
 
Norman Swan: So tell us about the use of these antipsychotics and why you
were worried enough to do this study? Because people raise a sign of the cross
to these antipsychotics in aged care and people with dementia. You're talking
about a very different group of people here, but they are poisonous in aged care.

Meera Agar: We were I suppose interested in this area because as clinicians we
see the distress that delirium causes for our patients and their families and us as
the treating clinicians. But we were looking at the evidence, and though
antipsychotics have been trialled in this situation they haven't been compared to
what we also are doing at that time which is treating all these underlying causes,
trying to explain to people what delirium is, but a lot of other supportive measures
that we can do to help people remain oriented to the environment, and we
wanted to see whether adding an antipsychotic on top of doing all of those other
things that we should be doing added any extra value to just doing those things
that we know are effective.

Norman Swan: So in other words this was a comparison against best palliative
care.

Meera Agar: Yes.

Norman Swan: And of course there is a misconception about palliative care in
the community, they think it's just about doling out narcotics to make people's
pain better, but really it's about comprehensive symptom management.

Meera Agar: And we know in hospitals seemingly simple things like having
people have their glasses on, their hearing aids with batteries, helping them have
a glass of water, helping them walk around the ward, these are things that often
get missed in the busy hospital environments that we work in.

Norman Swan: So you did a randomised trial, and there were two drugs,
haloperidol and risperidone. What do you find?

Meera Agar: So we found that after 72 hours of treatment where we allowed
people to increase the dose if distress continued, that the people in the
risperidone and haloperidol arms had worse symptoms than the people in the
placebo arm.
 
Norman Swan: Worse symptoms? To what extent?

Meera Agar: So, it was a small extent, but we were actually wanting to see a
benefit. So it was in completely the opposite direction to if the drugs were actually
helping reduce distress.

Norman Swan: And you found that haloperidol actually shortened survival?

Meera Agar: So we found in the antipsychotic arms the survival was 1.5%...the
people in the antipsychotic arms had a 1.5 times reduced survival than the
people in the placebo arm.

Norman Swan: So a 50% increase in the risk of death. What was causing that?

Meera Agar: We're not sure. These were people that were only receiving six
doses over a 72-hour period. It's possible because of the delirium not being
relieved that that may have led to worsened mortality, but we don't know whether
they had longer term exposure to these drugs after the study period.

Norman Swan: Another drug that is handed out like Smarties in this sort of
situation is olanzapine. Why didn't you study olanzapine?

Meera Agar: I suppose this was a very difficult trial to do and I think we had to
pick medications which are commonly used in this situation…

Norman Swan: But olanzapine is very commonly used.

Meera Agar: …and we also needed a matching placebo that could be matched
to both the active agents, and both risperidone and haloperidol come in an oral
solution, and haloperidol is the most commonly used medication for delirium.

Norman Swan: And what would you expect olanzapine to show in this sort of
situation?

Meera Agar: We would expect that it's quite a similar effect. These are
medications in a class, and the fact that we found both haloperidol and
risperidone showed these difficulties, we would expect that other antipsychotics
may also show problems with symptom control.
 
Norman Swan: And is there any indication of brain damage? In other words, that
by giving these drugs you're actually changing things in the longer term? Or was
it very immediate, the effect?

Meera Agar: So we started to see a difference in the symptom relief, even at day
one. How that is modulated at a neurotransmitter level is not well understood.
Delirium is a condition where the basic science of what actually causes delirium
is quite poorly understood.

Norman Swan: So the key here is for family and friends to notice delirium, it's a
change in cognitive state, and if that happens, too quiet or too active, they've got
to draw people's attention to it, but the solution is not the drugs.

Meera Agar: Yes, we need to be speaking to our patients and families and taking
changes in cognition or behaviour really seriously, and respecting that if they
have noticed a change then we need to pay attention and listen and respond
quite quickly.

Norman Swan: Meera, thanks for joining us.

Meera Agar: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Meera Agar is a palliative medicine physician at the
Centre for Cardio Vascular and Chronic Care at the University of Technology,
Sydney.

According to the National Mental Health Commission (that's the national body
that is supposed to keep governments honest when it comes to mental health
care in Australia), poor mental health costs the nation around $60 billion a year,
an astounding figure. The Commission also argues that there are investments
that could recoup some of that waste. To that end they brought out to Australia
an expert in such economic data. He is Professor Martin Knapp of the London
School of Economics and Political Science, LSE. Martin is in our Melbourne
studio. Welcome to Australia.

Martin Knapp: Thank you very much.

Norman Swan: So $60 billion is a lot of money.
 
Martin Knapp: Yes, it's a lot of money, and I think some of it is very well spent
and some of it is probably not so appropriately spent. I think part of the difficulty
with mental health issues is that quite often the way that we respond to
them…we have to respond to crises, and some of those costs would also be
outside the health sector for things that perhaps we could have avoided, like
contact with criminal justice or unemployment and so on. So I think there's a mix
of what I would call a good costs and bad costs in there.

Norman Swan: There's a two-away relationship between mental health problems
and the economy. Poor economic circumstances can cause…just take us
through the two-way relationship.

Martin Knapp: Okay. Well, certainly it is the case that people who are in very
difficult circumstances, in poverty, who are facing long periods of unemployment,
who have unmanageable debt are at greater risk of getting mental health
problems, and those problems staying around for a long time. But it's also the
case that people who have those mental health problems will then have
difficulties in getting a job or earning a decent income, forming relationships and
so on. So it's a kind of two-way street, and it can for many people be a vicious
cycle. They lose their job, they become stressed, that makes it harder for them to
get a job and things just get worse and worse.

Norman Swan: Now, the bean counters in Canberra are used to lobby
organisations coming up with economic reports, arthritis, mental health, cancer,
blah, blah, blah, and they say, oh, it's just another access economics report and
put it to one side because they all say it costs a fortune, and if only you'd spend
money on it, life would be better and you'd save a fortune, which is just the trap I
fell into in my introduction. How much of this is bull and how much is real?

Martin Knapp: A lot of this is real. Certainly the costs are real. I think what we're
trying to emphasise in the discussions I've been having…I've been here for a
week now, I've managed to pick up an Australian cold at the time, but in the
period I've been here it's emphasising that there are ways in which these mental
health problems can be responded to or they can be prevented, and there's very
strong evidence from lots of places, including from the UK, that that makes a lot
of economic sense. So we are trying to emphasise that it's not just a big number
but it's a number that can be brought down if we can do something, particularly if
 
it's earlier in life or early in the course of the illness, to prevent it or to respond
very quickly.

Norman Swan: So let's look at some of these economic studies that you and
others have done in the UK. One is the things you can do in the emergency
department.

Martin Knapp: Yes, one of the things that we are very concerned with in the UK
and I'm sure it's the same here, is that many people who present to the
emergency department, perhaps after some self-harming, they might get patched
up by the emergency department but they don't get the psychosocial support
they really need. And what we've…not a study we've done but we found other
people's studies that have shown that if you can provide a bit of psychosocial
support within the emergency department…

Norman Swan: What does that mean actually?

Martin Knapp: Well, it's actually firstly just recognising there might be something
behind that injury which is reflecting a cry for help. Somebody really is feeling
very stressed, it might be a suicide attempt, it might just be a cry for help. Can
you get that person into contact with services, maybe you can actually direct
them into the services within the hospital setting, depending on how severe their
problem is. But when you do that the evidence shows it's very positive in terms of
preventing further such episodes for that individual and that also makes
economic sense too.

Norman Swan: So a fairly brief intervention…

Martin Knapp: Yes, I think it's just recognising it. Emergency departments, in the
UK at least, they are incredibly stressful environments, they are very, very busy,
you can understand the difficulties for staff. But if you can just find a way, it may
need a little bit of investment of a specialist in that setting, a way of actually
identifying these people and responding to their very desperate needs
sometimes, that can make a lot of sense.

Norman Swan: And maternal mental health, mother's mental health?
 
Martin Knapp: Well, maternal mental health I think is a global issue in that
probably half the cases of maternal mental health problems during pregnancy in
the early months after the birth don't get recognised and therefore don't get
treated. That's very bad for the mother of course but it's particularly bad for the
child because maternal mental health problems, postnatal depression is the most
common that don't get treated can lead to the child having emotional difficulties,
behavioural problems, lower intelligence. And so what we've done in one of our
studies is shown how those consequences through the child are very expensive.

We did a study two years ago, we just counted up those costs, but I think it was
sufficiently shocking to the UK government that they then invested a lot of extra
money in maternal mental health services. And what we've done subsequently is
then shown our National Health Service in England what they can do in terms of
better services for those mothers.

Norman Swan: And does that make a difference?

Martin Knapp: Well, there are interventions around that have been worked on,
they can be quite low level, just helping community professionals to identify
problems and respond to them. They might be more heavy duty, when a mother
has a psychosis and they need much more concentrated support. They do seem
to work in terms of improving the mother's mental health, and that will improve
the mother's attachment and engagement with the child and that should improve
the child's development.

Norman Swan: And briefly, you've also looked at bullying?

Martin Knapp: Yes, bullying I think is one of these problems, again, across the
world. We've shown that bullying in teenage years can lead to mental health
problems and mental health costs, even 40 years later. So people at 50 who
were bullied at aged seven show differences in their mental health and their use
of services compared to those who weren't bullied at age seven. So I think if we
can do something about that we would head off a lot of problems and costs.

Norman Swan: Those are just three areas. There's a lot of emphasis in Australia
in, say, early intervention in psychosis that might lead to schizophrenia. Are there
enough studies around to make these…to look at the whole area of mental
health and interventions, to really make the case for treasuries?
 
Martin Knapp: Well, I think there's a number of areas where we have got good
evidence. Still loads more research is needed, but I think I can point to evidence
across the lifespan, and it's also interventions not just in the health sector, it's
things that can be done in schools, in workplaces, in communities, to prevent
some of these problems occurring or responding very speedily when they do
emerge.

Norman Swan: Martin Knapp, who is professor of social policy, and director of
the Personal Social Services Research Unit at the London School of Economics
and Political Science.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, I look forward to your
company next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, how the quality of your diet is probably more important
than obsessing on the individual parts of it. Drugs in palliative care which make
distress worse and can even kill you. An investment strategy for the government
which could tap into potential earnings of around $60 billion. Not bad money
when the bean counters are looking for every cent. And how optimism can save
your life. A 70,000-person study has linked optimism to around a 30% reduction
in the risk of premature death from any cause. The lead author is Eric Kim of the
Harvard School of Public Health in Boston. Welcome to the Health Report.

Eric Kim: Thank you.

Norman Swan: What did we know about optimism and its relation to life
expectancy, dying prematurely, before you did your study?

Eric Kim: There have been studies linking optimism with reduced risk of death
from coronary heart disease, cardiovascular outcomes. However there has never
been a study looking at different causative outcomes as well.

Norman Swan: We should have explained this at the beginning, but we think we
know what optimism is but maybe you should just explain it.

Eric Kim: In a nutshell it's the expectation that things will be better than worse,
and what's really interesting is that people think that optimistic people are just
always chipper and sunny people. However, what's also interesting is that people
might not necessarily present that way but have just the internal belief that things
will get better.

Norman Swan: So they're not necessarily happy chappies?

Eric Kim: Yes, but do believe things will get better.

Norman Swan: This is the Nurses' Study, which we've had on the Health
Report many times over the years. It's an extraordinary large study, tens of
thousands of women followed over decades, and you've obviously done a
psychological profile on these women and seen what happens to them.

Eric Kim: There's a well validated optimism measure, and it asks questions like
'in uncertain times I usually expect the best', or 'I hardly ever expect things to go

my way', and there are a series of questions like this and you can assess
someone's level of optimism. And then we have looked and tracked people's
survival over time as well as lots of other factors.

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Eric Kim: We found that when we looked at people with the highest optimism
versus the lowest lowest optimism, so the top 25 versus the bottom 25, the most
optimistic had about a 29% reduced risk of mortality, and we also controlled for
all kinds of different confounders and saw that the association kept persisting.

Norman Swan: When you say reduced risk of mortality, mortality is 100%, so
you're talking about reduced mortality at your particular age?

Eric Kim: Yes.

Norman Swan: Now we've got to dissect optimism, because some people who
are pessimistic are depressed.

Eric Kim: Yes. I also want to say something that I'm very passionate about and
have seen a little bit of, this idea of potential victim blaming. People can have low
optimism for all variety of reasons, some that are within our control, but also a lot
of factors that are not within our control such as parental warmth when someone
is younger actually predicts someone's optimism. Levels of education and wealth
is weak but it is a predictor of optimism as well.

Norman Swan: So I'm assuming with parental warmth you're talking about the
emotionally in-tune parent who sets limits but within a loving environment.

Eric Kim: Yes, something like that.

Norman Swan: And how much of it is genetic or really pre-programmed into your
personality?

Eric Kim: There has been some twin studies and it shows that about 25% of it is
heritable, which suggests that there are things that we can do to influence our
levels of optimism.

Norman Swan: So you've adjusted for all these things, your diet, whether you
are depressed, and you still find that optimism by itself seems to reduce your risk
particularly of heart disease and cancer and other causes of premature death.

Eric Kim: Yes.

Norman Swan: So what is it about optimism that does it?

Eric Kim: There are three potential pathways, and one is that optimism may
influence better health, for example. Past studies have shown that optimistic
people actually eat healthier, exercise more and acquire better sleep. And a
second pathway might be that optimists have better coping skills, and there is a
recent review of over 50 studies and they showed that optimists in general use
better coping methods, like they seek support more in stressful times, they plan
for challenges and they have more contingency plans, like if plan A doesn't go
well, then they plan for B and C. And the third potential pathway is that optimism
may actually directly influence our biology.

Norman Swan: It's that last one we've looked at a couple of times on the Health
Report, particularly looking at people who have already got cancer, and this
comes to your caveat a few moments ago which is that you can blame the
person for not being optimistic. So they looked at people with cancer in Australia
and then tracked them through according to their attitude, their mental attitude,
are they optimistic or pessimistic, and it made absolutely no difference to the
outcome once you had cancer because one of the problems is that if your cancer
comes back people say, oh well, you didn't have a positive enough attitude.

Eric Kim: I'm not aware of that particular study but these were healthier people
at baseline, and we weren't looking at people who had serious illnesses, so that
might be a different subset.

Norman Swan: So when you find this sort of association in a study like this, it's
not necessarily cause and effect. You try and find out whether it is but really all
you can say is the link is strong between optimism and a 30% reduced risk of
dying prematurely from all-cause mortality. So that's fine. But it's not cause and
effect yet. To prove it's cause and effect you change somebody from a
pessimistic attitude towards life to an optimistic view. Is there any evidence at all
that changing one's view of the world and life changes your mortality rate?

Eric Kim: I think there were three studies published in JAMA Internal Medicine,
and I'll tell you an example of one of them. There were people who had a heart
condition, they had a heart procedure, and over the period of a year they induced
positive emotions in one group, and the other half had standard of care. And in
the group were they induced positive emotions they were actually 1.7 times more
likely to achieve their physician recommended levels of physical activity. And the
other studies actually showed higher medication adherence and things like that.
So there are some really promising and interesting randomised control studies
where we can pinpoint causality, showing that when we induce these positive
mental states, that it could change our health behaviours.

Norman Swan: And are there reliable techniques for switching you to the
optimism mode?

Eric Kim: There are some easier ones that have smaller effect sizes and then
more time and resource intensive ones that have larger effect sizes and are more
reliable. I'll start with the easier ones first. One is just listing things that you are
grateful for every day, and randomised studies show that if you do it for seven
days then your optimism will increase a little bit. Another showed that if you list
things that you do that are kind over a period of 14 days, that could also increase
your optimism a bit.

Norman Swan: Where you have been kind to somebody else?

Eric Kim: Yes, listing your instances of kindness throughout the day. And then a
third one is called the best possible self, and you think about your different
domains of life, whether it be…maybe one domain is your relationship with your
partner or spouse, another one is your career and another one is your
friendships, and you think about the best possible outcome. Then the next six
days you vividly try to imagine that, that has also been shown to increase
optimism a bit. Some of the more resource and time intensive ones include
mindfulness meditation, different forms of cognitive behavioural therapy, and
something called hope therapy.

Norman Swan: So those require a bit more work but they do have a larger
effect.

Eric Kim: Yes.

Norman Swan: Eric Kim, thank you very much for joining us on the Health
Report.

Eric Kim: Thank you so much.

Norman Swan: Eric Kim is at the Harvard School of Public Health in Boston.

And in a related story be sure to listen to the next episode of All in the Mind when

leads to chronic disease, and how having a sense of meaning in life can be
protective against disease. That's on Sunday afternoon at 5 o'clock and online on
Radio National.

Meantime you're with the Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio, and CBC

Let's stay with keeping your mortal coil as healthy as possible for as long as
possible and move from your mind to your diet. Australian research has found
that focusing on your whole diet rather than obsessing on individual nutrients
pays off in terms of obesity and blood pressure, and that our official dietary
guidelines do seem to work, which no doubt has a lot of experts breathing a sigh
of relief. The bad news is that you still have to stay off junk food. Katherine
Livingstone of Deakin University did a lot of the work on this study and she is in
our Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Katherine Livingstone: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Why choose obesity and blood pressure?

Katherine Livingstone: So obesity and hypertension are really major health
problems facing the average Australia population. We know, for example, two in
every three adults are overweight or obese, and one in every three adults have
hypertension, and it is really potentially quite interesting, the relationship between
risk of obesity and hypertension and the combined effect, so up to 75% of
hypertension is thought to be caused by being overweight or obese. So if we are
able to understand how we can tackle these major health issues we can really

make a meaningful impact on the overall health of the population. Of course one
of the ways we can do this, as you said, is through diet.

Norman Swan: So you looked at the extent to which people…just tell us about
this study that you did.

Katherine Livingstone: So in this study we were looking at individuals following
the Australian dietary guidelines. As many of your listeners will know, the
Australian dietary guidelines provide really useful key information on the types
and the amounts of the foods that we should eat to promote health and well-
being. And I think what's really important to distinguish in these
recommendations is that we have things that we should eat more of in our diet,
so these are the beautiful fruits and the vegetables and the whole grains, and
things that we should limit, so things high in saturated fat and salt, so these
would be our crisps and our biscuits. And so these are fantastic clear messages
to the public. But what's really missing is evaluating how are these updated
recommendations that were issued in 2013 actually relate to these major health
problems of obesity and high blood pressure.

Norman Swan: So what did you find?

Katherine Livingstone: So in our study we included just under 5,000 men and
women, and it's important to know that these were individuals from all across
Australia, so all states and territories, really great, fantastic nationally
representative data, and we derived two overall dietary scores, and these were
both based on the Australian dietary guidelines but there's quite an important
difference in these two scores. So the first one is based on whether individuals
meet the recommendations for what they should eat more of, so these are the
fruits and the vegetables, but also what they should eat less of, so these are high
fat cakes and crisps for example. Whereas the second score we actually looked
at what would happen if individuals just met the recommended foods, so if they
just ate two portions of fruit, five of the vegetables, they matched their intakes of
wholegrain, of lean meats and low fat dairy. And actually what we saw was a
really important differentiation between these two scores, in that individuals were
only associated with lower risk of obesity if they had both recommended intakes
of the things that they should eat more off and the things that they should eat
less of. So this is an important message to the public.

Norman Swan: So it wasn't just that you could feel honourable by having your
two fruits and five veg or…I can't remember which way around it is, but that sort
of thing, and not much red meat and low saturated fat, you had to stay off the
rubbish.

Katherine Livingstone: That's right. So people really have to consider, yes,
we've had great amounts of fruit and vegetables but that doesn't mean that there
is an excuse then to go out and eat a whole block of chocolate. We've got to
keep that message of moderation in mind.

Norman Swan: So where does the dietary pattern fit into this? Because people
obsess, you know, something which we recorded for the Health Report at the
Sydney Writers Festival recently, we got 700 people or something in the
audience, we got them to put up their hands, how many are on a gluten-free diet,
and 80% put up their hands. How many are on low carbs, and 50% put up their
hands. People are obsessing on individual nutrients rather than the whole diet.
Presumably they are running the risk of not being on the right diet.

Katherine Livingstone: That's right, and there are a lot of what we call fad diets
or celebrity endorsed diets out there, and I think the key message coming from
this study is that simply by following these tried and tested scientifically robust
recommendations, that we are going to achieve a really great impact on
maintaining our weight and maintaining healthy blood pressure. So we shouldn't
be fixated, as you said, on these single foods and these single nutrients, and
that's what the focus of the revised 2013 Australian dietary guidelines was, much
more food based, overall diet based because, as you said, we don't just eat a
potato, we are going to eat that as part of a whole meal. We're going to have
maybe our vegetables and maybe our meat, and it's the impact of all of that
together that's important.

Norman Swan: And is there a translation to life expectancy here?

Katherine Livingstone: We didn't look at life expectancy particularly in this
study, but you would hope that with a lower risk of obesity and hypertension, that
that's going to have knock-on effects on life expectancy but we didn't look at that
specifically.

Norman Swan: And do we all have to then go to the National Health and Medical
Research Council's website to find out the dietary guidelines and go cross eyed,
or is there a simple way of doing this? People say it's the Mediterranean diet, not
a lot of red meat, white meat, monounsaturated fats et cetera, that sort of dietary
pattern. Is that what it all boils down to?

Katherine Livingstone: Yes, so the recommendations are up on the website, as
you said, but the key messages to the public is you really do want to have a wide
variety of foods, so great colours and different components in there. You want to
have plenty of vegetables, plenty of fruits, plenty of wholegrain foods, so for
example maybe once a week instead of having the white rice you'll have the
wholegrain rice, plenty of lean meat and eggs and legumes, low fat dairy
products and plenty of water. We are all tempted to maybe have the fizzy drink
now and then, maybe just swap that for water more often.

Norman Swan: And don't feel honourable and have a blowout.

Katherine Livingstone: Exactly, everything in moderation and balance.

Norman Swan: Katherine, thanks very much for joining us on the Health Report.

Katherine Livingstone: Thank you, it's a pleasure.

Norman Swan: Katherine Livingstone is in the Institute for Physical Activity and
Nutrition at Deakin University.

People who are receiving palliative care are understandably often really
distressed and that can manifest as confusion, disturbed communication and
even the feeling that you are hallucinating. That often gets doctors reaching for
drugs called antipsychotics, normally reserved for people with schizophrenia. But
these have been poorly researched in palliative care. A recent Australian study
though suggests that these medications may make distress worse and even
reduce survival. Meera Agar was the lead author. Meera is a palliative medicine
physician at the Centre for Cardiovascular and Chronic Care at the University of
Technology, Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report.

Meera Agar: Thank you.

Norman Swan: So just tell me the typical story here, the typical patient that
you're talking about.

Meera Agar: So we're talking about people with advanced illness where we know
there is no longer a cure for their underlying illness and that their life expectancy
is shortened. And we know that at least one in three of those people will have a
delirium episode at some point in their final months of life.

Norman Swan: So delirium being what I just described…maybe you should just
describe it in a bit more detail, because it is often missed by nursing and medical
staff.

Meera Agar: So delirium is a condition of the brain which is actually a medical
emergency. There are many medical issues that cause delirium, including
infection, changes in medication, changes in your body, metabolic states such as
liver or kidney failure. And what happens is a whole raft of symptoms, confusion,
agitation, hallucinations are often the most noticeable ones, but people's inability
to focus attention, inability to communicate, drowsiness are also a part of the
spectrum of delirium, and often those are the ones that get missed.

Norman Swan: So what you're saying is there are some symptoms…some
people can be acting out and seeing things and really being very distressed and
outward and hard to control in some ways, and other people can go very quiet.

Meera Agar: And sometimes it's just assumed that because these people have
an advanced illness, that it's okay to have a day where you are a bit quiet and a
bit down, and people often don't think that it might be delirium that's causing
those sudden changes.

Norman Swan: And when you say it's a medical emergency, why is it a medical
emergency?

Meera Agar: Because we need to actually try and assess what the underlying
medical condition is very quickly and get on top of those issues. So if someone
has an infection causing their delirium, we need to be trying to treat that quickly
and expediently because the longer it has effects on the brain, the poorer the
outcomes for the delirium will be.

Norman Swan: So tell us about the use of these antipsychotics and why you
were worried enough to do this study? Because people raise a sign of the cross
to these antipsychotics in aged care and people with dementia. You're talking
about a very different group of people here, but they are poisonous in aged care.

Meera Agar: We were I suppose interested in this area because as clinicians we
see the distress that delirium causes for our patients and their families and us as
the treating clinicians. But we were looking at the evidence, and though
antipsychotics have been trialled in this situation they haven't been compared to
what we also are doing at that time which is treating all these underlying causes,
trying to explain to people what delirium is, but a lot of other supportive measures
that we can do to help people remain oriented to the environment, and we
wanted to see whether adding an antipsychotic on top of doing all of those other
things that we should be doing added any extra value to just doing those things
that we know are effective.

Norman Swan: So in other words this was a comparison against best palliative
care.

Meera Agar: Yes.

Norman Swan: And of course there is a misconception about palliative care in
the community, they think it's just about doling out narcotics to make people's
pain better, but really it's about comprehensive symptom management.

Meera Agar: And we know in hospitals seemingly simple things like having
people have their glasses on, their hearing aids with batteries, helping them have
a glass of water, helping them walk around the ward, these are things that often
get missed in the busy hospital environments that we work in.

Norman Swan: So you did a randomised trial, and there were two drugs,
haloperidol and risperidone. What do you find?

Meera Agar: So we found that after 72 hours of treatment where we allowed
people to increase the dose if distress continued, that the people in the
risperidone and haloperidol arms had worse symptoms than the people in the
placebo arm.

Norman Swan: Worse symptoms? To what extent?

Meera Agar: So, it was a small extent, but we were actually wanting to see a
benefit. So it was in completely the opposite direction to if the drugs were actually
helping reduce distress.

Norman Swan: And you found that haloperidol actually shortened survival?

Meera Agar: So we found in the antipsychotic arms the survival was 1.5%...the
people in the antipsychotic arms had a 1.5 times reduced survival than the
people in the placebo arm.

Norman Swan: So a 50% increase in the risk of death. What was causing that?

Meera Agar: We're not sure. These were people that were only receiving six
doses over a 72-hour period. It's possible because of the delirium not being
relieved that that may have led to worsened mortality, but we don't know whether
they had longer term exposure to these drugs after the study period.

Norman Swan: Another drug that is handed out like Smarties in this sort of
situation is olanzapine. Why didn't you study olanzapine?

Meera Agar: I suppose this was a very difficult trial to do and I think we had to
pick medications which are commonly used in this situation…

Norman Swan: But olanzapine is very commonly used.

Meera Agar: …and we also needed a matching placebo that could be matched
to both the active agents, and both risperidone and haloperidol come in an oral
solution, and haloperidol is the most commonly used medication for delirium.

Norman Swan: And what would you expect olanzapine to show in this sort of
situation?

Meera Agar: We would expect that it's quite a similar effect. These are
medications in a class, and the fact that we found both haloperidol and
risperidone showed these difficulties, we would expect that other antipsychotics
may also show problems with symptom control.

Norman Swan: And is there any indication of brain damage? In other words, that
by giving these drugs you're actually changing things in the longer term? Or was
it very immediate, the effect?

Meera Agar: So we started to see a difference in the symptom relief, even at day
one. How that is modulated at a neurotransmitter level is not well understood.
Delirium is a condition where the basic science of what actually causes delirium
is quite poorly understood.

Norman Swan: So the key here is for family and friends to notice delirium, it's a
change in cognitive state, and if that happens, too quiet or too active, they've got
to draw people's attention to it, but the solution is not the drugs.

Meera Agar: Yes, we need to be speaking to our patients and families and taking
changes in cognition or behaviour really seriously, and respecting that if they
have noticed a change then we need to pay attention and listen and respond
quite quickly.

Norman Swan: Meera, thanks for joining us.

Meera Agar: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Professor Meera Agar is a palliative medicine physician at the
Centre for Cardio Vascular and Chronic Care at the University of Technology,
Sydney.

According to the National Mental Health Commission (that's the national body
that is supposed to keep governments honest when it comes to mental health
care in Australia), poor mental health costs the nation around $60 billion a year,
an astounding figure. The Commission also argues that there are investments
that could recoup some of that waste. To that end they brought out to Australia
an expert in such economic data. He is Professor Martin Knapp of the London
School of Economics and Political Science, LSE. Martin is in our Melbourne
studio. Welcome to Australia.

Martin Knapp: Thank you very much.

Norman Swan: So $60 billion is a lot of money.

Martin Knapp: Yes, it's a lot of money, and I think some of it is very well spent
and some of it is probably not so appropriately spent. I think part of the difficulty
with mental health issues is that quite often the way that we respond to
them…we have to respond to crises, and some of those costs would also be
outside the health sector for things that perhaps we could have avoided, like
contact with criminal justice or unemployment and so on. So I think there's a mix
of what I would call a good costs and bad costs in there.

Norman Swan: There's a two-away relationship between mental health problems
and the economy. Poor economic circumstances can cause…just take us
through the two-way relationship.

Martin Knapp: Okay. Well, certainly it is the case that people who are in very
difficult circumstances, in poverty, who are facing long periods of unemployment,
who have unmanageable debt are at greater risk of getting mental health
problems, and those problems staying around for a long time. But it's also the
case that people who have those mental health problems will then have
difficulties in getting a job or earning a decent income, forming relationships and
so on. So it's a kind of two-way street, and it can for many people be a vicious
cycle. They lose their job, they become stressed, that makes it harder for them to
get a job and things just get worse and worse.

Norman Swan: Now, the bean counters in Canberra are used to lobby
organisations coming up with economic reports, arthritis, mental health, cancer,
blah, blah, blah, and they say, oh, it's just another access economics report and
put it to one side because they all say it costs a fortune, and if only you'd spend
money on it, life would be better and you'd save a fortune, which is just the trap I
fell into in my introduction. How much of this is bull and how much is real?

Martin Knapp: A lot of this is real. Certainly the costs are real. I think what we're
trying to emphasise in the discussions I've been having…I've been here for a
week now, I've managed to pick up an Australian cold at the time, but in the
period I've been here it's emphasising that there are ways in which these mental
health problems can be responded to or they can be prevented, and there's very
strong evidence from lots of places, including from the UK, that that makes a lot
of economic sense. So we are trying to emphasise that it's not just a big number
but it's a number that can be brought down if we can do something, particularly if

it's earlier in life or early in the course of the illness, to prevent it or to respond
very quickly.

Norman Swan: So let's look at some of these economic studies that you and
others have done in the UK. One is the things you can do in the emergency
department.

Martin Knapp: Yes, one of the things that we are very concerned with in the UK
and I'm sure it's the same here, is that many people who present to the
emergency department, perhaps after some self-harming, they might get patched
up by the emergency department but they don't get the psychosocial support
they really need. And what we've…not a study we've done but we found other
people's studies that have shown that if you can provide a bit of psychosocial
support within the emergency department…

Norman Swan: What does that mean actually?

Martin Knapp: Well, it's actually firstly just recognising there might be something
behind that injury which is reflecting a cry for help. Somebody really is feeling
very stressed, it might be a suicide attempt, it might just be a cry for help. Can
you get that person into contact with services, maybe you can actually direct
them into the services within the hospital setting, depending on how severe their
problem is. But when you do that the evidence shows it's very positive in terms of
preventing further such episodes for that individual and that also makes
economic sense too.

Norman Swan: So a fairly brief intervention…

Martin Knapp: Yes, I think it's just recognising it. Emergency departments, in the
UK at least, they are incredibly stressful environments, they are very, very busy,
you can understand the difficulties for staff. But if you can just find a way, it may
need a little bit of investment of a specialist in that setting, a way of actually
identifying these people and responding to their very desperate needs
sometimes, that can make a lot of sense.

Norman Swan: And maternal mental health, mother's mental health?

Martin Knapp: Well, maternal mental health I think is a global issue in that
probably half the cases of maternal mental health problems during pregnancy in
the early months after the birth don't get recognised and therefore don't get
treated. That's very bad for the mother of course but it's particularly bad for the
child because maternal mental health problems, postnatal depression is the most
common that don't get treated can lead to the child having emotional difficulties,
behavioural problems, lower intelligence. And so what we've done in one of our
studies is shown how those consequences through the child are very expensive.

We did a study two years ago, we just counted up those costs, but I think it was
sufficiently shocking to the UK government that they then invested a lot of extra
money in maternal mental health services. And what we've done subsequently is
then shown our National Health Service in England what they can do in terms of
better services for those mothers.

Norman Swan: And does that make a difference?

Martin Knapp: Well, there are interventions around that have been worked on,
they can be quite low level, just helping community professionals to identify
problems and respond to them. They might be more heavy duty, when a mother
has a psychosis and they need much more concentrated support. They do seem
to work in terms of improving the mother's mental health, and that will improve
the mother's attachment and engagement with the child and that should improve
the child's development.

Norman Swan: And briefly, you've also looked at bullying?

Martin Knapp: Yes, bullying I think is one of these problems, again, across the
world. We've shown that bullying in teenage years can lead to mental health
problems and mental health costs, even 40 years later. So people at 50 who
were bullied at aged seven show differences in their mental health and their use
of services compared to those who weren't bullied at age seven. So I think if we
can do something about that we would head off a lot of problems and costs.

Norman Swan: Those are just three areas. There's a lot of emphasis in Australia
in, say, early intervention in psychosis that might lead to schizophrenia. Are there
enough studies around to make these…to look at the whole area of mental
health and interventions, to really make the case for treasuries?

Martin Knapp: Well, I think there's a number of areas where we have got good
evidence. Still loads more research is needed, but I think I can point to evidence
across the lifespan, and it's also interventions not just in the health sector, it's
things that can be done in schools, in workplaces, in communities, to prevent
some of these problems occurring or responding very speedily when they do
emerge.

Norman Swan: Martin Knapp, who is professor of social policy, and director of
the Personal Social Services Research Unit at the London School of Economics
and Political Science.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, I look forward to your
company next week.
